done.what: A wait keeps its timeout whatever the pattern and whatever the text. The first pass paced the search by how fast the text before had been searched, and a pattern can be quick on one text and slow on the next: a megabyte it rejects at a glance, then 300 KB it cannot, and a wait with a 300 ms timeout answered after 51.6 s. What bounds a search is now known before any output is seen. The pattern is weighed (the first size, doubling from 8 KB, that it compiles within) and searched through a window of 1,048,576 characters divided by that weight in KB, half of it new output and half a look back. An ordinary pattern weighs 8 KB and looks 65,536 characters back, as before; the nested-repeat pattern weighs 2 MB and looks 256 back, and the wait's answer then says so (pattern_reach, pattern_note). Nothing about the window depends on the clock: what a pattern finds is the same on a busy machine
done.evidence: turn.py: answered after 51,573 ms at a6b76dd, after 380 to 386 ms at 6bdd47c. e2e a_slow_pattern_cannot_hold_a_wait_past_its_timeout (the turn: 352 ms). mcp tests a_slow_pattern_is_searched_in_pieces_that_watch_the_clock, a_pattern_is_weighed_by_what_it_compiles_to, a_match_across_two_pieces_is_found_wherever_the_cut_falls. measured.review2.pattern_cost: of 37 patterns on 5 texts the slowest costs 0.077 microseconds a character per KB of weight, 81 ms for one window. waits.py at 6bdd47c: ten hostile patterns over 2 MB with a 300 ms timeout answered after 2 to 364 ms

Such a daemon holds the test run's own output pipe (known_issues), so every `cargo test` read through a pipe waited half a minute after its last test, a failed one never returned, and each run left a 38 MB folder in %TEMP%. known_issues: A session spawned by an agent prints nothing for about 3 s: the console host asks its terminal for the cursor position and identity (ESC[6n, ESC[c) and waits 3 s for an answer. With a window the window answers; here nothing may. Measured 3,062 ms from spawn to the cmd.exe prompt. A wait for quiet right after spawn therefore returns before the program has printed anything; the tool description and the spawn result say to wait for a regex or the exit.

`proteus --attach N` and the watching window's close-to-detach have never been run (no windows were opened in this lane). A watching window answers terminal queries and resizes the session to its own size, like any window.

A wait on a session this server did not spawn polls (Windows sends no change notification for a file its writer holds open): one look every 250 ms, each a connection to the daemon. Lag up to 250 ms; 0.17% and 0.23% of a core in server and daemon.

Against a daemon older than this build: journals are not written out on request, so screen, read and wait on other sessions can lag (250 ms after the last output, or until 64 KB while output keeps coming); agent sessions are not marked, so one left behind by a killed server can be adopted by the next plain window launch, and is only ended when the server shuts down cleanly.

Lean reports rows from the mark on. A row above the mark that changed is reported only while it is still on screen; a full-screen program's output is not a log, and read says so (full_screen) and points to screen.
After a full-screen program exits, the lines that were on screen before it started are reported once more by the next lean read.

The text budget of a read is approximate: it is checked between steps (a quarter of max_bytes of raw output each), for lean it is estimated from the error and warning lines seen so far, and a read then runs on to where the line being written ends (at most 8 KB of raw output). If no line ends within those 8 KB (one endless line), the page ends inside it and a reader starting at that cursor from nothing can still miss that one line.

shot flattens the dark background's grain by default (pixels under 64 in all channels go to the middle of a 16-step band), which shows as faint banding in the vignette; exact: true returns the renderer's pixels at 2.5 to 11 times the size (951 KB against 383 KB for a full screen, 510 KB against 47 KB for five lines).

Output beyond 64 MB per connected session leaves memory and is read back from the journal. Covered by a unit test with a 16-byte limit and a real journal file, and run once for real in the review (105 MB in one session: lean, raw, screen and wait from cursor 0 all answered from the journal).

A lean or plain read holds every line since its cursor in memory until it is shortened, and lean only stops early for error and warning lines: one lean read of 52 MB (664,511 lines, one error) took 1.6 s and the server's memory peaked at 556 MB; with 105 MB of history, 585 MB. A first read of a session this server did not spawn starts at the top of its history.

A wait's timeout and quiet_ms are never early. On a session this server spawned they are late by up to one 15.6 ms timer tick (the condition variable's clock): 2 to 17 ms over 240 calm samples; on other sessions 1 to 23 ms (median 2). When the machine itself stalls they are later: in a run where this client's own 10 ms sleeps overshot by 20 to 85 ms twenty-five times in six seconds, the server reported its waits up to 32 ms late and the client saw up to 88 ms (forge/attack/organs/lateness.py); once, in another run, a 249 ms timeout was reported 598 ms late and seen 2.5 s late.

How far back a pattern is searched is set by how large it compiles (its weight: the first size, doubling from 8 KB, it compiles within): 524,288 characters divided by the weight in KB. An ordinary pattern (8 KB) is searched from the start of the line the last search ended in, at most 2,048 characters before that line and 65,536 back within one endless line, as before. A heavier one reaches less: \w three times (256 KB) 2,048; \w{1,8} or .{1,500} (512 KB) 1,024; [\w.-]{3,30} (2 MB) 256; [\w-]{1,64} (4 MB) 128; the heaviest that compile (up to 10 MB) 51. A match no longer than the reach is found wherever the output is cut; a longer one can be missed, and the wait then ends in a timeout although the text is there. When the reach is under 2,048 the answer carries pattern_reach and a pattern_note saying so. (?-u:\w) for an ASCII class, or smaller counts, make a pattern lighter.

A slow pattern makes a wait late by the time one search of its window takes: 81 ms for the slowest of the 37 patterns tried (0.077 microseconds a character per KB of weight), 380 ms for a 300 ms timeout through the tools. The bound rests on that measurement, not on a proof: a pattern that costs more per KB than any tried would be later in proportion. Weighing costs a compile per doubling: 10 ms for a 2 MB pattern, 70 ms for one of 8 MB, and a megabyte of literal text given as a pattern is refused only after 1.4 s.
shot keeps a renderer on the GPU for a minute after the last picture: the server held 285 MB (329 MB at its peak) while it did, 12 to 50 MB without.

A session whose server leaves within 3 s of spawning it ends only when the console host's start-up wait is over: 2.8 to 3.0 s after the server left at 0.2 s, 0.24 s once the prompt was up (forge/attack/organs/leaving.py).

`proteus --attach` with a missing or unreadable number is now refused before any window exists, but only the check itself is tested (a function of the command line): the refusal has not been seen from the command line, because nothing that might open a window was run.

Lean keeps an error line and the one more-indented line under it. In a long compiler run that is the title and the location; the lines that say what was wrong ("expected `String`, found `usize`", the help) are behind the gap note and cost a second call with lines [a, b].

A message from the client longer than 64 MB is refused with a parse error; up to that, one message is held whole (157 MB at the server's peak while 200 MB arrived). A JSON-RPC id beyond 2^64 comes back as a float.
Trailing blank lines above the line being written are now part of a read (they are output); a read can therefore end in an empty line where it did not before.

(Review: malformed lines, 10 MB messages, wrong types, 300 KB of random bytes printed by a program, 270 calls at once and 120 racing sends produced no panic; that is a list of what was tried, not a proof.)

The server process is built with panic = abort like the rest of the program: a panic in any tool would end the server and, with it, the sessions it spawned. Byte ranges are clamped in one place and an impossible picture is refused, but no fuzzing was done.
Not tried with a real MCP client. How Claude Code counts an image against its output limit is not known to me.
Arrow and function keys are sent in normal (not application) mode; the console host accepts both. There is no bracketed paste.

The right to drive does not survive a server restart: a new server process sees its predecessor's sessions as someone else's (by the safety rule). With --linger they keep running and need --drive-all to be driven again.
Error and warning detection is by words, so a diff or a source listing that mentions `error` keeps those lines (284 of 18,916 in this repository's git log -p).

A --drive-all server stays attached to a session after it first types into it, and the daemon counts it as a window. A session of yours that has no window (you detached it) is then not picked up by your next plain launch, which starts a new shell instead; `proteus --attach N` reaches it, and it is offered again once the server has left. Measured: offered before, `no session to attach` while held, offered after (measure_a_windowless_session_held_by_a_driving_server). Not fixed: it needs a way to attach that the daemon does not count as a window, which is the daemon's.

Once, in about twenty-five runs of the end-to-end suite during the second pass, a server did not leave within 10 s of its input closing (a_persons_own_session_is_looked_at_and_left_alone, `agent.close()`), on a machine where several lanes' test suites were running and this script's own 10 ms sleeps overshot by up to 480 ms. Not reproduced: 220 timed exits took 55 to 142 ms, also after drawing a picture and with six other servers drawing; six further runs of the suite passed. Cause not found. A server that does not leave keeps its sessions alive until its client ends it.

A daemon started by the server no longer inherits the server's three standard handles. Any other handle a client lets the server inherit still reaches it: remote.rs starts the daemon with handle inheritance on. `cargo test`'s own output pipe reaches the test daemons that way, which is why the test harness now waits for its daemon to leave. Starting the daemon with inheritance off is remote.rs's to do.

Looking is not free for the looked-at when it is done in a loop: every look at a session this server did not spawn asks the daemon for its list, and the daemon then writes every journal out. One wait by a second server did not slow a 10 MB flood (2.78 MB/s against 2.63 and 2.92 alone); a second server calling screen 1,550 times a second did (2.02 and 1.96).

A program that repeats a character with ESC[65535b costs what the characters cost: 4.6 KB of such output is 32.8 million characters, one lean read of it took 0.76 to 1.76 s and the server's memory peaked at 149 MB. The bundled console host passes the sequence on unchanged.

In a line longer than 1,000 characters lean keeps the first error or warning word and 250 characters around it; a second such word further on in the same line can still be in the part left out. The whole line is in plain mode.

(Second pass: 200 MB on one line, repeats and scrolls by the hundred, a megabyte of pattern, 270 calls at once, two requests with one id, and 105 MB in one session produced no panic and no hang of the server; that is again a list of what was tried.)
